title: When an assumption becomes reality
dek: On the beliefs we stop noticing, and why it's worth asking where they came from.
body:
An assumption can become so deeply embedded in someone's understanding of reality that they no longer recognise it as one.

I think the culture we grow up in works this way. It isn't a neutral view of the world. It's closer to a shared story, built out of language, that we're born into and then mistake for reality itself. Every culture believes its version of how things are is the sanctioned one. It rarely is. It's just the version that culture happens to be running right now.

Sociologists reached a similar idea by a careful route. In The Social Construction of Reality (1966), Peter Berger and Thomas Luckmann argued that the everyday world we take for granted is built and maintained by people, then experienced as if it were simply given. What feels like reality is often an agreement we've stopped noticing.

Very few of our beliefs are formed entirely independently. Much of what we consider normal, acceptable or simply true has been shaped by where we grew up, who we've surrounded ourselves with and what we've been exposed to.

Take success. For many people, a successful life means financial security, career progression, owning a home and the things that come with it. None of that is unreasonable. But we're also told that beauty comes with a nicer car and satisfaction with a bigger garage, and a lot of that is substitution: something to want in place of asking what we actually want. Where did the idea come from?

I can see it in my own path. By my early twenties I'd worked at a law firm in Melbourne, in IT support, in retail and at the New Zealand Film Commission, done a real estate qualification and started my own design studio. On paper it looks like range. Honestly, a lot of it was me trying on versions of success that other people would recognise: the professional office job, the career with a clear ladder. None of them quite fit, and it took me longer than I'd like to admit to ask why I was chasing them in the first place.

We rarely stop to examine these ideas. They're reinforced by school, advertising, popular culture, family expectations and the institutions we move through. Eventually a particular set of cultural values starts to feel like an objective measure of how a life should be lived. Culture isn't an enemy, but it isn't your friend either. It largely serves the convenience of the institutions that shape it, and it rarely asks what you actually want.

## Free thinking is a privilege

I'd go further than that. These markers of success aren't just absorbed over time. They're handed to us young, as if they were non-negotiable, long before we're old enough to question them.

And questioning them takes room. It's hard to think freely about what you want from life when you're worried about rent, food or where the next pay is coming from. Researchers who study scarcity have found something similar: in a 2013 study published in Science, sugarcane farmers in India did worse on cognitive tests before harvest, when money was tight, than after it. The researchers' explanation is that money worries take up mental space, leaving less for everything else. How large that effect is remains debated, but it matches what most people know from experience.

That makes free thinking something closer to a privilege than a given.

It isn't only about money, either. Even people from financially stable homes rarely get the space. At 18, most of us are pushed into something close to survival mode: choose a course, take on a loan, find a job, start proving yourself. It can feel less like the start of a life and more like an experiment, a test of whether you'll turn out to be a "success" by a definition you never chose. The question of what you actually want gets put off until there's time, and for many people there never is.

Developmental psychology has a name for those years. Jeffrey Arnett called the period after school "emerging adulthood", a stage defined by exploring who you are before adult roles settle in. His theory has been criticised for mainly describing middle-class, university-educated young people, and when Arnett tested it across social classes he found real differences, including in access to financial support for education. Even the time to work out who you are is unevenly shared.

## Who benefits from the default

Here's the uncomfortable part. The people who design the systems most of us live inside are, by and large, the people who did get the space to think freely: founders, executives, investors, policymakers. One large study of 1.2 million American inventors found that children from top 1% income families were ten times as likely to become inventors as children from below-median income families, and that early test scores explained relatively little of the gap. The researchers called the missing ones "lost Einsteins." The freedom to question and build is concentrated, and so is the power that comes with it.

The problem is that the incentives of the people running the system don't always line up with everyone else getting the same freedom. An attention economy needs people to keep scrolling. A consumer economy needs people to keep wanting the next marker of success. A labour market built on that 18-year-old test needs people too busy proving themselves to ask whether the test is worth passing.

None of this requires a conspiracy, and I don't think most people in those positions are trying to hold anyone back. It only requires incentives. When a system rewards you for other people staying on default, you don't have to plan for it. You just have little reason to change it. That's what makes free thinking political, not just personal. Enabling more people to question the defaults is good for them, and it's a risk to anyone whose business depends on those defaults holding.

## The network we were promised

When the internet arrived in everyday life in the 1990s, plenty of people expected it to dissolve boundaries rather than reinforce them. It would make us transparent to each other, a way of showing one another what's going on inside our heads. I find that a useful lens for any technology: does it dissolve boundaries, or maintain them?

Thirty years on, it's worth asking how that turned out.

In some ways the optimists were right. We can read academic research, international news and independent journalism, and hear from people whose lives are nothing like ours. But most of it now reaches us through privately owned platforms, where algorithms decide what we're likely to see. Those systems are built around attention, and attention is what they sell.

The research on what that does to us is more nuanced than the headlines. A 2017 study of more than 560,000 tweets found that each word that was both moral and emotional, like "greed," raised a political message's retweets by about 20%, and that the boost happened mostly within like-minded networks. Outrage travels, and it travels among people who already agree. Yet when researchers working with Meta moved consenting users onto a simple chronological feed during the 2020 US election, those users spent far less time on Facebook and Instagram, but their political attitudes didn't measurably change over three months.

So the algorithm's clearest effect may be on attention rather than belief. That's still an enormous amount of power, because attention is where beliefs get formed. And this is the incentive problem in practice. The Facebook Files, a 2021 Wall Street Journal investigation built on internal documents shared by whistleblower Frances Haugen, reported that the company's own researchers had raised concerns about Instagram's effect on teenage girls, while its public statements were more reassuring. The company knew enough to ask the question, and had commercial reasons not to act on the answer. It also decides what gets visibility and what data independent researchers can see.

Brave New World imagined a society kept calm with soma, a drug that meant nobody ever had to sit with a difficult thought. For decades, television was the closest thing we had. Swap television for the feed and the comparison lands harder. Television at least ended for the night. The feed is designed not to.

We usually talk about misinformation as people believing things that aren't true. We talk much less about what never reaches us at all. You can spend hours reading about world events and still have no idea what was filtered out before it got to you.

## And now AI

Machines have been making quiet decisions for decades: what gets ordered, what gets mined, who gets rostered on. AI moves that into language and judgement, the places where we actually do our thinking.

I'm not writing about it from the outside. I use these tools every day, and I've built things with them I couldn't have built alone. I've also watched them get good, fast, at the work I trained in. Design and web development are exactly the kinds of skills AI is learning quickest, and I've spent this year working out what my next move is because of it.

A system that can explain almost anything is also making choices: what it treats as the default, which framing it offers first, whose assumptions sit inside the data it learned from. It answers fluently either way, and fluency is easy to mistake for neutrality.

The same test applies. Does this technology dissolve boundaries or maintain them? An AI can widen what you're willing to consider, or quietly narrow it to the most common, most comfortable answer. Which one you get depends on who built it, what they're rewarded for, and how you use it.

There's a more personal side to this, too. For many people, work isn't just income. In 1982 the social psychologist Marie Jahoda argued that a job quietly gives us five things besides pay: structure to the day, social contact, a sense of collective purpose, status and identity, and regular activity. A study of a representative German sample later backed her model for four of the five. If AI takes over a large share of that work, it won't only threaten livelihoods. It will expose an assumption most of us never chose: that our purpose is our job.

I think that's where the real work is. We need to help people let go of what they've been told their purpose is, and ask what it actually is. But that brings it back to privilege. Asking someone to rethink their sense of meaning while they're worried about paying the bills is asking for free thinking without the conditions that make it possible. Helping people release those assumptions has to include giving them the security to think it through, even when that's inconvenient for the people who benefit from the old ones.

## Access isn't understanding

I keep coming back to the difference between having access to information and being able to form an independent understanding of it.

We tend to treat confidence as knowledge, familiarity as understanding and consensus as truth. None of those are interchangeable. An idea doesn't become true because we've heard it a thousand times, and a belief doesn't become ours just because we can explain it.

I'm wary of ideology of any kind. Once you adopt one, you already have the answers, and you no longer need your own mind. Not every shared belief is a trap, but the risk is the same whether the answers come from a doctrine, a feed or a chatbot: we stop doing the thinking ourselves.

I'm not suggesting we question everything or throw out the assumptions that help us get through a day. But here is a small habit worth trying. When a belief feels obvious, ask three things.

1. Where did I first hear this?

2. Who benefits if I keep believing it?

3. What's the strongest case against it?

You won't always like the answers. That's not the point. The point is that the belief becomes yours rather than something you inherited without noticing.

Which brings me back to where I started. Maybe a secure career, a home and financial stability really are what you want. If so, good. The difference is that it's a choice instead of a default. The harder part is making sure more people get the space to make it.

I think it's time we took back our minds. We were promised a network that would let us see inside each other's heads. Mostly, it shows us the inside of our own, over and over.

If the technologies we're building can give us access to more information than any generation before us, we should expect more from them than a mirror. Otherwise, are we simply becoming better informed about the things we've already been conditioned to believe?

## Sources

Several ideas in this essay, including culture as a shared reality built from language, technology as something that either dissolves or maintains boundaries, and the call to take back our minds, draw on Terence McKenna's talks and writing.
